You might think a man with 104 pole positions would not be too excited about one more, but Lewis Hamilton – never one to hide his mood – was bouncing up and down with joy at the conclusion of Qualifying yesterday, much like he did 20 seasons ago, when bagging his first.

No.105 has been a long time coming. His first for Ferrari, three years and a team change after his last for Mercedes.

The good news for Hamilton in his quest for victory is that practice suggested overtaking in Sunday's race is going to be very difficult. The bad news is that it’s an awfully long way to Turn 1, and he’s going to be towing a pack of highly motivated rivals all the way down to the braking point.

George Russell starts P2, with Charles Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli on the second row, while Max Verstappen and Lando Norris are on row three. They’re all winners this season, and while Antonelli has reason to be a little more circumspect, the others are here to add to their tally. The race is tantalisingly poised between one stop and two, which is going to make it very interesting indeed.

title: How F1 drivers and teams have embraced Dia de Muertos
excerpt:
The Mexico City Grand Prix is renowned for its passionate crowds, colourful paddock and spectacular celebrations. But this year, the race takes place during one of Mexico's most important cultural occasions – Dia de Muertos, or Day of the Dead.

Taking place around the beginning of November, Dia de Muertos is a time for families to remember loved ones who have passed away and is traditionally marked through decorated altars, food, flowers and celebrations that bring communities together.

For Formula 1, the celebration has become a familiar part of its annual visit to the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez. Drivers have embraced the occasion through special helmets, elaborate face paint and even cooking challenges, while the paddock has welcomed performers and displays inspired by Mexican traditions.

As the 2026 race weekend coincides with Dia de Muertos, here's a closer look at the celebration, the meanings behind its most recognisable customs and how they have made their mark on F1.

What is Dia de Muertos?

Although its name might suggest otherwise, Dia de Muertos is as much a celebration of life as it is a remembrance of death. Rooted in pre-Hispanic traditions that later became intertwined with Catholic observances introduced by the Spanish, the celebration centres on the belief that deceased loved ones can temporarily return to the world of the living. While customs differ between communities, 1 November is commonly associated with remembering children who have passed, while 2 November is dedicated to deceased adults.

Rather than being an occasion solely for mourning, Dia de Muertos provides families with an opportunity to reconnect with those they have lost through their favourite foods, personal belongings and shared memories. Homes and cemeteries are typically decorated with flowers, candles and offerings, while relatives gather to celebrate the lives of their loved ones. Its cultural significance was recognised by UNESCO when the tradition was proclaimed in 2003, before being inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.

When Dia de Muertos inspires the drivers' helmets

Special helmets have become a regular feature of the Mexico City Grand Prix, with drivers using the occasion to incorporate Mexican artwork into their designs.

In 2024, Carlos Sainz unveiled a Dia de Muertos-inspired helmet featuring a colourful skull motif across the crown. The design also incorporated a chilli pepper, referencing his long-standing nickname. The Spaniard went on to win the race for Ferrari, making it a memorable helmet for his collection.

Sainz was not the only driver incorporating the occasion into his race weekend that year, with Pierre Gasly also opting for a special design featuring Dia de Muertos-inspired imagery. However, few drivers have embraced Mexican heritage through their helmet designs as consistently as Sergio Perez.

For his home race in 2022, the Red Bull driver unveiled a design featuring La Catrina, an elegantly dressed skeletal figure who has become one of the most recognisable symbols associated with the festivities. The helmet also incorporated papel picado, the decorative paper banners traditionally created by cutting intricate patterns into sheets of coloured tissue paper.

La Catrina has a fascinating history of her own. The figure emerged through the work of Mexican printmaker Jose Guadalupe Posada, whose satirical skeletal imagery was later popularised by the artist Diego Rivera. Today, she appears throughout Dia de Muertos celebrations, with her distinctive hat and elaborate clothing inspiring everything from face paint to enormous public installations.

The following year, Perez unveiled another helmet created by Mexican artist Karla Lozano, whose winning design incorporated papel picado, alebrijes and other cultural references to Mexico and his home state of Jalisco. While alebrijes belong to a wider tradition of Mexican folk art, they have also become familiar sights at contemporary Dia de Muertos celebrations.

The paddock gets a Dia de Muertos makeover

Over the years, the Mexico City Grand Prix paddock has become almost as colourful as the celebrations taking place across the capital.

Anyone who remembers the 2016 Mexico City Grand Prix might recall a rather unusual appearance by Red Bull team mates Max Verstappen and Daniel Ricciardo. Arriving for their Thursday media commitments, the pair were almost unrecognisable beneath elaborate skull-inspired face paint, embracing the imagery associated with Dia de Muertos. Mercedes also joined in with the festivities that year, decorating their hospitality area to mark the occasion.

The colourful skeletal designs worn by the Red Bull drivers echoed the calavera, or skull, imagery commonly seen during Dia de Muertos. Skulls appear in various forms during Día de Muertos, including decorative artwork, face paint and sugar skulls known as calaveras de azucar.

The tradition has continued at subsequent races. In 2024, drivers entering the paddock were welcomed by performers dressed as Catrinas, who handed out cempasuchil flowers, the bright orange Mexican marigolds closely associated with Dia de Muertos. Charles Leclerc made a particularly memorable entrance in a traditional charro-style outfit associated with mariachi musicians, carrying one of the flowers given to him on arrival.

Cempasuchil flowers are traditionally used to help guide the spirits of deceased loved ones back to their families, with petals often arranged along pathways leading towards altars.

A taste of Mexico

Food is central to Dia de Muertos, and it has also provided Formula 1 drivers with some rather entertaining experiences away from the track. During the 2024 Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, Oscar Piastri swapped racing duties for food preparation, making guacamole alongside a Dia de Muertos performer in the paddock.

While guacamole itself is not specific to the celebration, food plays an important role in Dia de Muertos, with families preparing dishes enjoyed by deceased relatives and placing them on ofrendas.

These offerings vary depending on the individual being remembered and the traditions of each family, with everything from tamales and mole to fruit, sweets and favourite drinks appearing alongside photographs and personal possessions.

Perhaps the most recognisable seasonal speciality is pan de muerto, a traditional sweet bread prepared around Dia de Muertos. Often flavoured with orange blossom or citrus and topped with sugar, some versions feature dough decorations shaped to resemble bones.

Recipes differ across Mexico, with regional varieties and contemporary fillings adding to the range available in bakeries during October and November. This year, the Mexico City Grand Prix organisers have confirmed that visitors will be able to sample different versions at the circuit, including traditional sugar-coated breads and filled alternatives.

Ofrendas and the meaning behind the celebrations

While the colourful costumes, special helmets and paddock activities have become familiar features of the Mexico City Grand Prix, one of the central Dia de Muertos traditions is the ofrenda.

These altars, created in homes, cemeteries and public spaces, are dedicated to deceased loved ones, bringing together photographs, personal belongings and offerings that reflect the lives of those being remembered.

For the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix, organisers have confirmed that an altar de muertos will be installed in the circuit's Blue Zone, dedicated to members of the motorsport community who have passed away.

It marks a particularly poignant addition to this year's race weekend, offering a connection between Mexico's tradition of remembrance and the people who have helped shape the sport's history.

With the Grand Prix taking place on 1 November, the display also serves as a reminder of the significance behind the festivities that have become such a recognisable part of F1's annual visit. Beyond the elaborate artwork and celebrations, Dia de Muertos remains an occasion for honouring those who are no longer here, ensuring their memories continue to be shared.

title: ‘This experience has shaped me’ – Gasly on his work with Make-A-Wish
excerpt:
Following on from Formula 1’s first sport-wide Social Impact Report, where it was announced that more than 500,000 young people across 71 countries had benefitted from Formula 1’s charitable programmes in 2025, F1.com speaks to Alpine driver and Make-a-Wish France Ambassador Pierre Gasly about his work with the charity – with F1 having helped to make over 50 wishes come true last year for children living with critical illnesses.

One experience in particular from Gasly’s ambassadorship with the Make-A-Wish Foundation has stayed with him. The French driver was giving a tour of Alpine’s Enstone factory in the UK to a 17-year-old boy living with a critical illness.

“I took him around the factory in an Alpine A110 road car, and he could name every single car model that we crossed paths with on the road: the year, the engine, the horsepower. And I was, like, mind-blown – like, ‘I should be the car guy here and I'm clearly not!’ His knowledge about cars was insane, and he was so positive – a very bright personality… I felt pleased that I could make it happen.”

Within two months, Gasly’s guest at Alpine that day had passed away from his illness. If Gasly had been convinced of the Make-A-Wish Foundation’s worth when he became an ambassador for the charity back in 2023, it was that experience that made it hit home even more.

The Make-A-Wish Foundation’s roots run all the way back to 1979, when a seven-year-old child from Scottsdale, Arizona called Chris Greicius was diagnosed with leukaemia. With the help of his local community, Chris had his wish of being a police officer for a day granted, taking a police helicopter tour of Phoenix while wearing his own special uniform, and getting sworn in as Arizona’s first and only honorary Department of Public Safety member. And sadly, just like Gasly’s guest at Enstone, Chris would die a short time later from his cancer. The Make-a-Wish Foundation was born from Chris’ experience.

Like most young drivers coming into Formula 1, Gasly’s primary focus in his first seasons in the sport were beating his team mates and building his reputation with stand-out performances on track. But once established in the paddock, Gasly quickly realised that he wanted to start using his position to make a positive impact on the world.

“I remember having the conversation with my manager, and I told him that I'd like to find ways of giving back and actually being more involved with this sort of charity work – to just involve myself,” says Gasly. “Make-a-Wish felt like a good fit.

“I think it's a lot about trying to find ways to give back to people, thanks to the chance I have to be in the position that I am in Formula 1,” he adds. “Experiences I've had with Make-A-Wish and seeing the impact that I could have on these kids has been absolutely incredible.

“It's just very fulfilling as a human to feel that I can positively impact [these kids] – and it doesn't matter at the end of the day whether you impact one million people's lives or one, as long as I can do something positive and actually have a positive action and support someone, I find it very special.”

Gasly’s activities with the charity have ranged from auctioning off helmets to meeting kids at track, with Gasly clear that the positive impact of these meetings flows both ways.

“I would say this experience has shaped me,” he says of his ambassadorship. “I've had a fair few experiences that have made me stronger in the way that I approach and look at things.”

Formula 1 publishes first sport-wide Social Impact Report

Asked by F1.com if he ever struggles to contain his emotions when meeting these kids and hearing their stories, often just moments before jumping into his racing car, he pauses before replying: “Not to say that I don't get affected because I'm someone who is quite emotional – and at the end of the day it's definitely tough to see the reality as it is.

“But I would say it just makes you reflect quite a lot on your life, on people's lives, and the chance that we have to live in the conditions that we live in.

“Some of these kids, already from a very young age, they know that unfortunately, they won't have the same chance and they won't have same amount of time as we get. So it definitely makes you reflect on a few things in life.

“I think it’s had a real impact on my life, on appreciating everything we have. Because it's so easy to complain about small stuff but… we should not allow ourselves to complain when we see the chance that we have to live our lives.”

While Gasly’s high profile as an F1 driver is helping to raise awareness of the Make-a-Wish Foundation, the Alpine driver is adamant that everyone and anyone can contribute to help make kids’ wishes come true…

“I always say there is no small or big donation,” says Gasly. “Any donation is used for these wishes and to realise the dreams for these kids who are obviously facing unique conditions. And that's why I always encourage people to donate.

“Sometimes you think two euros, five euros, 10 euros won't make a difference, but the reality is when you're talking a hundred, or a thousand people making a five-euro donation, it does change the life of hundreds of kids.

“People also wonder, ‘Where is my donation going to go? Does it actually impact anything?’ I think in the position that I am in as an ambassador, I can say that all these donations actually go to these kids and do change their lives and impact their lives very positively.

“And when you see the impact – and I’ve had the chance to see it live, right in front of me, how beneficial it is for these kids to actually get to live an incredible moment that they've dreamed of their entire life – you just realise it's worth everything.”

title: Alonso's 'frustration is beyond imagination' after issues
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has stated that his "frustration is beyond imagination" after a power unit problem brought the Aston Martin driver's Qualifying for the Mexico City Grand Prix to an early end.

Alonso was robbed of the chance to show what he could do by a painful power unit issue early in Q1 after what had been a reliable weekend for him up to that point, with the team explaining a suspected water pressure issue linked to the ERS system was the cause.

The Spaniard finished Friday’s Free Practice 2 session in P12, just 0.769s off the pacesetting Ferrari of Charles Leclerc, a margin that suggested that he was very much in the midfield fight.

Alonso put in a good first lap to top the times in the opening minutes of the session but then received an urgent radio message from the Aston Martin pit wall to stop the car, which he did just short of the pit lane entrance before visibly showing his frustration.

“It was 100 metres away from the garage, but probably the problem was bigger than anything possible to do in the garage," he said.

"So yeah, the safest thing for everyone else also on track was to stop – and I followed the instruction.”

Asked if he’d been optimistic after that strong Friday showing, the two-time World Champion replied with: “I was…”

However, that didn’t quite extend to a place in Q3 being a realistic possibility, although a decent result was lost.

“Probably difficult, but [in practice] we were P12, P13, P11, so we were in the window. If we put a good lap, maybe it was possible, but I think that was probably too optimistic. Maybe P13, P12 was our position today.”

Mexico has proved better suited to the AMR26 package compared to other tracks than had been anticipated, and Alonso said there was a simple reason.

"Less straights. There are two straights only into [Turn] 1, into 4. The rest, with the level of grip so low, you hardly can go full throttle, so there is less power sensitivity here. So it was maybe because of that.”

The experienced Spaniard is pessimistic about the chances of making progress from P18 on the grid at a track where running in traffic is notoriously challenging.

“Huge problems with temperatures for everybody,” he said. “When you start at the back, there is no way you can follow cars closely, or something like that.

"So, there is not much we can do – and I think we lost a big opportunity. So frustration is beyond imagination. But this is the story of the year.”

title: Who is F1’s latest debutant Ryo Hirakawa?
excerpt:
Following a number of Free Practice 1 appearances, Ryo Hirakawa will make his F1 race debut at the Mexico City Grand Prix after Haas announced on Saturday morning that the Japanese racer would replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the event. Here is everything you need to know about Formula 1’s latest debutant…

Gaining experience across different categories

After beginning his career by participating in karting championships in his native Japan, Hirakawa graduated to single-seaters in 2010.

From there he progressed through categories including Formula Challenge Japan and the Japanese Formula 3 Championship, winning his debut race in the latter before going on to seal the 2012 title.

Hirakawa’s next step saw him move to Super Formula in 2013, having joined the Toyota Young Driver Program. He would go on to score four wins and four pole positions across his nine years racing in the category.

The Japanese driver also competed in Super GT in the GT500 class between 2014 and 2021, a series in which he won the title in 2017.

World Endurance Championship success

Hirakawa’s racing experience expanded further when he joined the World Endurance Championship in the Hypercar class from 2022 with Toyota Gazoo Racing.

Success quickly followed, as the driver from Japan went on to win the Drivers’ Championship in his maiden season alongside team mates Sebastien Buemi and Brendon Hartley. The squad repeated the feat again in 2023, and also scored a second consecutive 24 Hours of Le Mans triumph.

Hirakawa continues to compete in the series, where the Toyota Racing team are currently leading the 2026 standings.

Arriving into Formula 1

It was announced in September 2023 that Hirakawa had joined the McLaren Driver Development programme and would also become a reserve driver for the outfit. He went on to compete in his maiden FP1 session with the squad at the 2024 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Hirakawa subsequently moved to Alpine for 2025 as a test and reserve driver, with his second FP1 appearance coming at the Japanese Grand Prix – but the now 32-year-old switched to Haas soon afterwards.

This led to four further practice runs in 2025 followed by another two in 2026 – with the second coming just before an unexpected call-up to the main team…

F1’s oldest debutant since 2014

One day after taking the wheel of Ocon’s car during FP1 in Mexico City, Haas released a statement confirming that Hirakawa would replace the Frenchman for the remainder of the weekend.

This makes the Japanese driver the oldest debutant in the sport since Andre Lotterer back in 2014, who was also 32 when he entered the Belgian Grand Prix for what would be his sole F1 event.

Lotterer’s day quickly came to an end when his Caterham suffered a mechanical issue just one lap in – but Hirakawa, who qualified in 19th place for his maiden event, will surely be hoping for better on Sunday in Mexico City.

title: F1’s longest pole career spans as Hamilton returns to top
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton scored his 105th pole position at the Mexico City Grand Prix, extending his own record as the driver with the longest pole position career span, coming over 19 years after his maiden top spot in Formula 1. We take a look at the top 10 drivers with the longest career spans between their first and last poles.

10. Sir Jack Brabham – 10 years, 9 months, 1 day

Sir Jack Brabham’s first pole position came in Britain, in 1959, back when Aintree Racecourse was a sporadic host of the country’s Grand Prix. Brabham enjoyed prolific success through the 1960s, founding his own team and becoming the only driver to win a World Championship while doing so, and his last pole position came in 1970 at the Spanish Grand Prix, when it was held at the tight and fiddly Jarama track.

9. Sebastian Vettel – 11 years, 29 days

Sebastian Vettel was a renowned Qualifying specialist and dominated entire seasons, taking a record 15 poles from 19 attempts in his high watermark 2011 campaign with Red Bull Racing. His 57 pole positions, third on the all-time record list, were spread across 11 years. His maiden top spot came during the rain-drenched Monza session in 2008, where he stunned for Toro Rosso, and caused an even bigger upset by converting his grid position 24 hours later. Vettel’s last one-lap wonder came with Ferrari, at the classic figure-of-eight Suzuka Circuit in 2019, fittingly a track where he trumped his rivals on five separate occasions.

8. Giancarlo Fisichella – 11 years, 1 month, 4 days

Giancarlo Fisichella spent just two years in title-contending machinery, and consequently a return of four pole positions was a decent accomplishment, and both his first and last pole positions came as something of a surprise. Fisichella fronted a rain-hit session at the Red Bull Ring in 1998 while competing for Benetton, which was entrenched in the midfield, and spent the twilight of his career with backmarkers Force India. But at Spa-Francorchamps in 2009 the upgraded VJM02 was on form, and Fisichella stunned by storming to top spot in Qualifying – bearing in mind up until that stage the team had not scored a point since mid-2007.

7. Riccardo Patrese – 11 years, 5 months, 1 day

Riccardo Patrese competed for Arrows for several years and emerged on top in a closely-fought Qualifying battle against reigning champion Alan Jones at Long Beach in 1981. Patrese and Jones finished three-quarters of a second clear of the pack, and it was the Italian who edged the fight by just nine-thousandths of a second. The lion’s share of Patrese’s success came during his three-year stint with Williams from 1990 to 1992, though he was regularly shaded by Nigel Mansell. In 1992 Mansell took an astonishing 14 poles from 16 attempts in the iconic FW14B, leaving Patrese with just one to his name, in Hungary.

6. Michael Schumacher – 12 years, 2 months, 1 day

Now, this is a contentious one… Michael Schumacher would be bumped up to second place on this list if the criteria was drivers who led Qualifying, rather than drivers who had pole position. Schumacher’s maiden pole came in subdued circumstances in Monaco, in 1994, the first Grand Prix after the deaths of Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger. His last came in France, for Ferrari, in 2006 – but six years later for Mercedes he set the fastest time during qualifying in Monaco. However, a five-place grid penalty for causing a collision at the previous Grand Prix in Spain denied Schumacher the chance to start from pole position…

5. Alain Prost – 12 years, 2 months, 22 days

Alain Prost was famously more of a racer than a qualifier, particularly in an era where Senna was the one-lap king. Prost’s first pole came with Renault at Hockenheim in 1981, with the turbocharged RE30s flying around the circuit’s high-speed sections. Prost went on to take 13 of his 33 career poles in his final season, and only one in Williams colours, in 1993. The last of those was achieved at Suzuka – which was also his only pole position at the iconic venue.

4. Mario Andretti – 13 years, 11 months, 6 days

All-round racing icon Mario Andretti was due to compete at Monza in 1968 but a clashing commitment, and Italian regulations, denied him the chance to debut. Instead, he returned at Watkins Glen, where he set pole position for his proper debut, though mechanical issues scuppered a tilt at victory. Andretti’s last pole had looked set to be at the same venue, exactly 10 years later, but after he walked away following the 1981 season he made a handful of stand-in appearances in 1982. Replacing the injured Didier Pironi at Ferrari, Andretti scored an emotional pole position at Monza, just 0.035s ahead of Nelson Piquet.

3. Rubens Barrichello – 15 years, 1 month, 20 days

Rubens Barrichello had to wait until 2000 to score a long overdue maiden victory but his first pole position came in only his sophomore season in 1994, as a slick tyre gamble at a wet-but-drying Spa-Francorchamps paid dividends. It gave Jordan a maiden pole position and also ensured Barrichello became the then youngest ever polesitter. For a driver who adored his home Interlagos circuit it’s fitting that Barrichello’s last pole came there, for Brawn, in 2009 – his third at the circuit as the joint record-holder. Though, unfortunately for Barrichello, none of those Interlagos poles were converted into a victory.

2. Kimi Räikkönen – 15 years, 2 months, 4 days

Kimi Räikkönen was fast from the outset in Formula 1 but after three near-misses he finally scored his maiden pole position at the Nurburgring’s European Grand Prix in 2003. More poles followed for McLaren and Ferrari, but after a two-year hiatus, and two years with Lotus, Räikkönen finally ended a nine-year drought in Monaco, in 2017, with a striking lap around the Principality. There was one more flier, on Ferrari’s home turf in 2018, 15 years after his first pole, and it proved to be Räikkönen’s last time atop the leaderboard on a Saturday.

1. Lewis Hamilton – 19 years, 4 months, 22 days

When Lewis Hamilton hammered the McLaren MP4-22 across the final chicane in Montreal and gunned for the line in 2007 he secured his maiden pole at only the sixth time of asking. It was to be the first of 105 – and counting. Hamilton’s peak came in 2016, when he scored 12 of the available pole positions, and he also claimed a double-digit number of pole positions in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2020. It was a leaner return in the ground effect era, with Hamilton topping Grand Prix Qualifying only once, in Hungary, in 2023. Ferrari’s difficult 2025 consigned Hamilton to a frustrating year, but greater competitiveness in 2026 has yielded a stronger campaign, including in Qualifying. Hamilton already held the record for the longest time between first and last – or should we say, most recent – poles, but that now stands at an extended 19 years, 4 months, and 22 days, after his effort in Q3 in Mexico City.

title: 5 late-notice F1 debutants and how they fared
excerpt:
Ryo Hirakawa will make his Formula 1 debut at this weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix after being drafted in by Haas to replace Esteban Ocon. Hirakawa, 32, will climb into the VF-26 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez in order to make a relatively short-notice debut, having also run in FP1, but how have other short-term debutants fared in Formula 1?

Stephane Sarrazin – 1999 Brazilian GP

Stephane Sarrazin had a solid junior single-seater career, coming in sixth place in International Formula 3000 in 1998, which was regarded as the final step towards Formula 1 back then.

He was also a test driver for Prost, but it was with Minardi whom he made his debut in Brazil having been drafted in for Luca Badoer, when the Italian regular suffered a wrist injury.

Sarrazin qualified a respectable 18th, ahead of team mate Marc Gene, though in the race had a dramatic accident midway through proceedings when he went off through the final corner at high speed.

Sarrazin looped the Minardi several times before coming to a safe halt, ending what proved to be his first and only F1 race.

Sarrazin went on to have an eclectic and varied career in motorsport, including in sportscars, rallying and Formula E, winning the pre-WEC Le Mans Series in 2007 and 2010.

Hirakawa to replace Ocon at Haas for Mexico City Grand Prix

Andre Lotterer – 2014 Belgian GP

Andre Lotterer was a Jaguar test driver in the early 2000s but the German instead found a plethora of success elsewhere. Lotterer won titles in Japan, in Super GT and Super Formula, won the first World Endurance Championship in 2012, and claimed three victories at Le Mans – including in 2014.

A few weeks after that third triumph Lotterer was drafted in by the ailing Caterham squad, which had undergone ownership and management changes, for the first post-summer break Grand Prix in Belgium.

Caterham’s slow and underdeveloped CT05 was a hopeless cause, but Lotterer fared well, out-qualifying regular Marcus Ericsson in wet conditions.

The race, though, was a short-lived encounter as a mechanical problem halted Lotterer after only the first lap, and regular racer Kamui Kobayashi was restored to the line-up thereafter. Lotterer returned to sportscars – and Formula E – and he added another WEC title in 2024, before moving to Genesis for the brand’s debut campaign.

Stoffel Vandoorne – 2016 Bahrain GP

Stoffel Vandoorne was McLaren’s reserve driver in 2016 off the back of an emphatic title-winning campaign in the GP2 Series the previous year.

McLaren kept Vandoorne active with a seat in Super Formula, and he was out in Japan preparing for the new campaign when he received the urgent call to fly across to Bahrain.

Regular racer Fernando Alonso had been ruled out of action in Bahrain in the aftermath of his violent crash at the opening round in Australia, when he rolled through the gravel after colliding with Esteban Gutierrez’s Haas.

Vandoorne took an overnight flight, during which he effectively read the manual of McLaren’s MP4-31, and he arrived in the country just a few hours before the first practice session. Vandoorne qualified in 12th position, ahead of team mate Jenson Button, and ran a solid race to round out the top 10 – picking up a point in the process.

Vandoorne secured an F1 seat with McLaren full-time, but was dropped after two years, though remained active in the sport through reserve roles at Mercedes and Aston Martin.

Nyck de Vries – 2022 Italian GP

Nyck de Vries had a circuitous route to F1, as the one-time McLaren protégé eventually won the Formula 2 title in 2019, by which time avenues to a race seat had not been forthcoming.

De Vries won the Formula E title with Mercedes, and picked up a reserve role at the team, and in 2022 fulfilled the young driver role for Mercedes and a couple of its customer teams: Aston Martin and Williams.

De Vries participated in FP1 at Monza for Aston Martin, as expected, but on Saturday found himself instead behind the wheel of Williams’ FW44 after Alex Albon was ruled out due to appendicitis.

From Salo to Bearman – 10 memorable F1 stand-in performances

The team’s package was strong around the high-speed blasts at Monza and de Vries profited handsomely, qualifying in 13th position, which became eighth on the grid due to various engine penalties elsewhere.

De Vries raced competently and picked up two points for ninth position, and his performance facilitated a full-time move to AlphaTauri for 2023.

However, it was a short-lived affair, as De Vries was dropped after 10 Grands Prix. De Vries returned to Formula E, and sportscars, where he this year triumphed for Toyota at the Le Mans 24 Hours.

Ollie Bearman – 2024 Saudi Arabian GP

Ollie Bearman had caught the eye in junior categories, and had Ferrari affiliation, and was in the early stages of his sophomore Formula 2 campaign in Saudi Arabia when he got a message on Saturday morning to hot-foot it to the F1 paddock.

Bearman, who had already taken pole position in Jeddah for the weekend’s Formula 2 race, was parachuted in to replace Carlos Sainz, after the Ferrari driver was taken unwell because of appendicitis.

Bearman got up to speed through the final practice session and qualified in 11th position, only narrowly missing out on a berth in Q3, and in the race went on to take a creditable seventh place – the youngest driver to score points for Ferrari.

Bearman made two more stand-in appearances in 2024 with Haas, and then joined the team full-time for 2025, where he has since remained – and will this weekend be team mate to debutant Hirakawa.

title: What the teams said – Qualifying in Mexico City

Ferrari

Ferrari have been quick all weekend, but it was Charles Leclerc who looked the pick of the two Scuderia cars. But come Q3, Lewis Hamilton was the one to nail his last lap when it mattered and make the most of the track evolution to grab a brilliant pole position. It is his first P1 start in a Grand Prix for Ferrari, as he hunts his second race win for the team. The oldest man to be on pole since Mario Andretti in 1982, Hamilton certainly stole some of Antonelli’s thunder on Saturday.

Leclerc had a scrappy final run in Q3, knowing pole was in his grasp. But he just could not get his tyres in the right working window and had to settle for a still decent P3, especially considering he starts on the clean side of the grid and will have a slipstream down to Turn 1.

Lewis Hamilton, 1st, 1:16.514

"It’s an incredibly special feeling to take my first pole position for Ferrari. I’ve been working towards a moment like this for a long time, so to finally achieve it means a lot. It hasn’t been a straightforward weekend, with the running we missed and the issue we had yesterday, but we took important lessons from the last race, made good progress with the setup, and today we brought it all together when it mattered.

"The margins are so fine, which makes this result all the more rewarding. A huge thank you to everyone at the track and back in Maranello. We can be proud of today, but of course, our focus now turns to tomorrow and converting this into a strong result for the team."

Charles Leclerc, 3rd, 1:16.633

"I think there was a bit more in it today. On the out-laps, it was quite difficult to put the tyres in the right window, and this was our biggest challenge. There's such low grip with the downforce that we have here in Mexico City, that you've got to push the car to the limit in these conditions, which is quite fun. On my second run in Q3, I had a clean out-lap, but at the end, I just didn't put the lap together. Starting third here is not too bad, so we will give it all and see what we can bring home for the team."

Fred Vasseur, Team Principal

"I am very happy for Lewis and for the whole team. His first pole position with Ferrari is an important milestone and a result that rewards all the work that has gone into it. This weekend, Lewis found the right balance between pushing and managing the tyres, and today it paid off. Charles had a good first run in Q3 and then made a small mistake on his last attempt, but P3 is still a good place to start from here.

"The most important part of the job, however, will be tomorrow. Both Lewis and Charles will be starting on the clean side and a lot will be about the race down to Turn 1, where the slipstream could play a big role. After the first lap, the key will be to try and be in clean air, as overheating in dirty air is an issue we all have to deal with. We now have to find the best strategy and execute a clean start, with both drivers working together as a team."

Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli wound up just 0.001s behind Norris in the final practice session, paving the way for the Italian to fight for pole. But Mercedes just did not seem to really have the pace in the early stages of Qualifying. While both cars comfortably made Q3, neither looked right in the mix. That is until the final laps, when George Russell pulled out something special to grab P2 on the grid. He wound up just 0.009s off pole, and is well placed to make a challenge for the victory to keep his slim chances in the title fight going.

As for Antonelli, he wound up fifth after struggling to warm up his tyres in Q3. But he starts fourth thanks to Verstappen’s penalty, and if he finishes there he will have done more than enough to take the World Championship crown.

Kimi Antonelli, 5th, 1:16.707

"It wasn’t my best qualifying today. I struggled to find the grip from the tyres in Q3 and didn’t put together the lap I wanted, with a few too many mistakes. It’s disappointing as I felt more comfortable earlier in the session and hoped we could be fighting further forward. That said, we’re still P4 and there is plenty to play for tomorrow.

"The run to Turn One is very long here, so getting a good start and staying out of trouble will be important. We’ve also saved a set of Soft tyres which could give us some options in the race. I think we have a good chance to fight for a strong result, so I’ll get some rest tonight, reset and focus on doing the best race we can tomorrow."

George Russell, 2nd, 1:16.523

"That wasn’t an easy session, but I was pleased with my final lap. It came together when it mattered and we were able to get a good result out of the session. It was tricky getting the tyres into the right window and we took a slightly different approach with our preparation compared to some of those around us. We opted to go for it on the first lap at the end of Q3, rather than take a preparation lap, and that proved the right call. The performance was clearly in the car, but we need to understand why we haven’t been able to access it as consistently as we would like recently.

"It’s very close between the four teams at the front, so tomorrow should be an interesting race. Overtaking will be difficult and managing the power unit and brake temperatures will be important, but we’ll see what opportunities come our way. My focus is on finishing the season strongly and maximising every opportunity we have."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"It was incredibly close out there today. The gap between Lewis (Hamilton) and George was probably no more than 50 centimetres on track, which shows how fine the margins were. It was a difficult session for us though overall. The tyre was tricky to get into the right window and the grip dropped away quickly, so getting the preparation right was important. George’s quickest lap came without a preparation lap, whereas we took a different approach with Kimi, so we need to look at that and understand whether we could have optimised it better.

"The race will be a different challenge. The margins were just as small on Friday’s long runs as we saw on the single lap today, so getting the start, strategy and tyre management right will be important. We are starting from a position where we can fight, and our focus will be on executing a clean race with both cars and seeing what opportunities come our way."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We had a relatively straightforward FP3, evaluating the changes we made overnight and doing some work to better understand the tyres on lower fuel. We made some progress with the set-up, although we were still struggling with a loose rear on corner entry and understeer at the apex of the slower corners. That made it difficult to put a complete lap together. Our pace on the Medium tyre wasn’t particularly strong, but the additional grip from the Soft helped and, by the end of the session, it looked like we might have the performance to fight for pole.

"We didn’t change much on either car going into qualifying, but it was a slightly messy start to the session, and we were lacking some pace early on. The track temperature continued to drop, which would normally help us, but after the first runs in Q2 we still looked to be a few tenths away. We improved as the session progressed and George produced a very strong final lap in Q3 to take a place on the front row, just a few milliseconds from pole. Kimi finished P5 and wasn’t especially happy with either the car or his own performance. With penalties applied, we will start P2 and P4 tomorrow. Given the long run to Turn One, that puts us in a reasonable position. Our long-run pace on Friday looked competitive, but managing brake and Power Unit temperatures is likely to be one of the key factors in the race. Both drivers can fight for the podium and, if we can manage those temperatures and use the performance in the car, hopefully we can be in the fight for the win too."

Red Bull

Max Verstappen qualified fourth in Mexico City, which at the start of the day he might have taken. But Red Bull got their car into a better working window for Qualifying, with the Dutchman in the mix throughout. His first run in Q3 was exceptionally quick, but he locked up on his final run through the stadium section which ended his charge. With his grid penalty, he starts fifth tomorrow.

Isack Hadjar was frustrated throughout the day with how his car was behaving, and he came close to missing out on Q2, leaving it very late to get a lap in. He aborted his first run in Q3 too after a lock up, but did manage to at least beat the midfield cars to grab seventh on the grid.

Max Verstappen, 4th, 1:16.692

“I think overall my Qualifying went really well. We improved the car a lot from practice and it was all coming together nicely for Pole. Unfortunately, I was in some dirty air and the car in front of me, instead of going left, was driving right. This meant I lost my reference, lost downforce and had the car in the wrong place for the braking point, so I locked up. It was a shame as I was for sure in the fight for Pole and it affected my lap. However, the most important thing for me was that the car was in the right window and that it will feel a lot better in the race tomorrow. Ultimately, it was really promising how we turned things around; it is quite tough to follow here but if you have a good race car then you can do something."

Isack Hadjar, 7th, 1:16.900

"I feel like I didn't do a good enough job today, I just couldn't get it to click throughout Qualifying. The car was very fast and we had real potential to be on Pole, so that's frustrating. I think I made too many mistakes. The pace was there, but I found it a little trickier to drive than in practice. I was locking up a lot, particularly into T13, and I just couldn't get a feel for the brakes. The Team has put in hard work to get the car to where it is and you always want to deliver for them. Starting from seventh isn't going to be easy, but a lot can happen in T1 and the race pace was looking promising. We'll need to make some early moves tomorrow, so let's see where we can end up."

Laurent Mekies, Team Principal

“After a bumpy start to the weekend, that was a good turnaround again today in Qualifying, so well done to everyone in the Team for coming together and making a strong improvement compared to where we were with the car yesterday. We had the pace to fight for the top positions this afternoon, even if the final lap in Q3 did not go to plan.

"On Max’s last attempt, he was the fastest on track up until the point where he got traffic from Lando in the last sector and lost the chance to fight for Pole, so that’s a shame. Isack showed strong pace as well and kept building throughout Qualifying. There was certainly the potential for more.

"For tomorrow, even if we start quite far back, we will try to put some pressure on our competitors and be ready to take any opportunities from what happens ahead of us. It is going to be a long race, extremely demanding on the chassis and PUs, and of course in terms of tyre management, so we look forward to the battles on track.”

McLaren

Lando Norris was fastest in final practice, and with Oscar Piastri not that much further back, hopes were high that McLaren could fight for pole. But they had a difficult Qualifying, with Piastri knocked out in Q2 for the first time this season. He ran used tyres initially in that segment which didn’t help, and then could not nail his last lap when the pressure was on.

Norris made Q3 with relative ease, but once there it did not go to plan. He admitted that there was nothing wrong with his last lap per se, he just could not quite get the car in the same working window as he managed when he topped the timing sheets in Q2.

Lando Norris, 6th, 1:16.824

"A challenging afternoon. My Q2 lap was incredibly strong, but it was unrealistic to expect a repeat of that in Q3 with the car currently not consistent enough from one run to the next, so putting together two strong laps is a real challenge. I don’t think we had more than this result available today as Pole wasn't within our reach.

"We’ll work towards tomorrow’s race now. We know that overtaking looks incredibly challenging with the speed limiter, but we’ll do our best to gain positions from sixth to secure strong points for the team."

Oscar Piastri, 13th, 1:17.646

"A frustrating Qualifying today. Up until Q2, we were in a really competitive position. The car felt well-balanced throughout Free Practice 3 and during the first phase of Qualifying, but the moment we fitted the new set of tyres, its behaviour completely changed. It was a bizarre situation after making only minor setup tweaks, so we’ll need to investigate thoroughly to understand what went wrong.

"Looking ahead to tomorrow's race, our objective remains to push forward and fight our way into the points. We know we have solid underlying race pace, but overtaking around this circuit will be extremely tough with the current straight-line speed characteristics and limited slipstream effect. It will require a calculated and determined drive through the field, but we will make the most of every opportunity to progress."

Andrea Stella, Team Principal

"A result that certainly leaves a bitter taste in our mouths. To be honest, we were hoping to secure two good positions on the starting grid, because our performance seemed to be better than what we’d seen in recent races, but the MCL40’s inconsistency let us down at the crucial moments. It happened first with Oscar in Q2, and it’s a shame because up until that point he’d shown himself to be very competitive, even on a track that’s certainly not best suited to his style. Then it was Lando’s turn on his second attempt in Q3, when a place in at least the first two rows was definitely within his reach.

"We know that when the drivers push this car to the absolute limit, its behaviour can sometimes be unpredictable, even more so when racing in windy conditions and on a slippery track: the slightest snap can easily result in a sudden loss of grip, which comes at a high cost. This makes the drivers’ task very difficult and demands flawless execution from the whole team: it’s up to us to put ourselves in the best possible position to showcase our pace, both in this final stage of the season and, above all, next season.

"For tomorrow, we’ll aim to make the most of the strong stamina we demonstrated in Free Practice to try and achieve the best possible result. Lando is still in a position to fight for a podium finish, whilst it’s clear that Oscar’s aim is to finish in the points and thus demonstrate that his progress can translate into a good result. The battle for third place is wide open, and we must do everything we can to secure at least that result."

Racing Bulls

Having looked the pick of the midfield all the way throughout practice, it was no surprise that Racing Bulls got both cars to Q3 with relative ease. They had two runs on fresh soft tyres, with Liam Lawson beating his team mate Arvid Lindblad by less than a tenth. The duo initially looked set to trade places thanks to Lawson's one place grid drop, until news broke that the Kiwi racer had been disqualified from Qualifying for a technical breach regarding his car's MGU-K deployment.

Liam Lawson, 8th, 1:17.029

“It feels good to have two cars finish in Q3 today. The penalty from yesterday means I'll be starting in P9, but it's positive for both of us to be leading the midfield. I apologised to Max after yesterday's incident as it was unnecessary. It's something I'll learn from moving forward, but we're now both focused on tomorrow. It's a tough track, but I love driving the car and I'm excited for the race where we'll be pushing for double points."

Arvid Lindblad, 9th, 1:17.117

"I don’t feel like I delivered as well as I could have today, and there was definitely more time to find. I found a really good rhythm in Q2, but unfortunately I wasn’t able to carry that into Q3 and didn’t deliver the laps I know I’m capable of. The team have done a great job with the set-up this weekend, and the drivability has definitely improved, so it’s disappointing not to have converted that into a higher starting position. I'm looking forward to the race tomorrow; we’re still starting from a good position and I think points are definitely within reach.”

Mattia Spini, Head of Trackside Engineering

"A very good Saturday for the team with both cars through to Q3 and ahead of our direct competitors. Both drivers struggled with the car balance in the low-speed section at the start of FP3, but we improved the behaviour throughout the session. By the end, they were more comfortable and setting competitive lap times, leaving only some fine-tuning ahead of qualifying.

“We expected Q1 to be challenging, with different run plans across the field, and the red flag in the middle of the session added another complication. We managed it well and got both cars into Q2 using just one set of tyres each. Arvid found a significant chunk of lap time on his first run in Q2, while Liam made his step on the second, securing a place in Q3 for both drivers. With Liam carrying a one-place grid penalty, it was important for him to qualify ahead, and he did exactly that. Our focus now turns to the race, where a good start and a strong opening lap will be paramount.”

Alpine

Pierre Gasly made it all the way to Q3 for the fourth time in the last five race weekends. He was only 0.036s off the pace of Lindblad ahead too which was encouraging, with Alpine looking to have lost ground in their fight with Racing Bulls of late, especially on pace. Franco Colapinto could not match his team mate but he did take 12th which is a decent starting slot.

Both will inherit a place thanks to Lawson's disqualification, enhancing the teams chance of points.

Pierre Gasly, 10th, 1:17.153

“I am happy to be in Q3 today. It's been tight all weekend in the midfield so we knew we would need to maximise everything in Q1 and Q2 to ensure we could advance to the top ten. I have no regrets in Q3, I gave it everything I had, and we just lack a couple of hundredths to Racing Bulls who seem to have a little bit on us at the moment. That has been a trend recently, so something for us to continue to work on and improve. After a positive day yesterday, Free Practice 3 was a little difficult, tyres were cold, I lacked grip, but that changed for Qualifying. It's a tight window to perform and it is difficult to get it right sometimes. Looking ahead to the race, it's a long run down to Turn 1 here and it's never an easy start. I will focus on what I can control and hopefully we can take the fight to Liam [Lawson] and Arvid [Lindblad] ahead and give them a hard time. Our race pace was good yesterday so of course our target has to be to score points.”

Franco Colapinto, 12th, 1:17.640

“I'm not super happy with today's result, as I thought there was more performance out there and the chance of possibly making it into Q3. I was not super comfortable in the car in Qualifying and it was tricky to get the best out of the tyres for the full lap. The start of the lap was good and felt strong but we were generally losing time as the lap went on, particularly in the tight final sector. The focus now is to do our best job in the race, where I think we're probably more competitive and consistent. We're usually quite good off the line and it's a very long run down to Turn 1 here. So, we'll look to make some places on the opening lap and go from there, with points again being the target for the team.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“Today's result is probably a fair reflection of our current level of competitiveness. After a positive day yesterday, we had some concern after Free Practice 3 with both drivers struggling more than we would have liked, especially with tyre preparation. We turned it around for Qualifying where both drivers did a good job in Q1 to progress, with Pierre saving a set of new Softs with an eye on tomorrow's race. Q2 was tight and Franco has been a little bit off Pierre on most runs this weekend, having more limitations on braking, and he lost some time in the final sector as the rears overheat and grip tends to lack. He is still in the mix for tomorrow starting P12 especially with the long run down to Turn 1 where I am sure he will be keen to put some pressure on those ahead. Pierre ended P10 where he had a good first run in Q3, and two thirds of his final lap were strong before a scrappier final sector, missing just a tenth or so to the Racing Bulls. He is eager for a good start tomorrow and he will try to make some moves ahead as we aim to have both cars scoring together.”

Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto missed most of FP2 with a car issue, and his luck did not change on Saturday. He was limited to just two laps in final practice with a PU issue, the team opting to change his engine for another one in his pool. Having also missed FP1 for Audi rookie Freddie Slater as the rookies got some laps in, the Brazilian was awfully short of lap time and did well to make it as far as he did. Nico Hulkenberg qualified a few places higher up, but could not quite make it to Q3. Nonetheless, the German will start in the top 10 thanks to Lawson's DSQ.

Nico Hulkenberg, 11th, 1:17.306

"It was a pretty good qualifying session overall. We made steady progress throughout, the laps were clean and I don't think there was much more left on the table. Of course, missing out on Q3 by just three hundredths is a bit of a shame, but that's how tight things are in the midfield. P11 isn't a bad place to start from, and we've also got a fresh set of soft tyres available, which could come in handy tomorrow.

"The race here is always a tough one, particularly when it comes to managing temperatures and cooling the power unit. We'll look at our strategy options tonight and see what we can make of it tomorrow."

Gabriel Bortoleto, 14th, 1:17.680

“It was a shame not to be able to take part in FP3 earlier today, but the mechanics have done an incredible job getting the car back together and ready for Qualifying, so I want to say a big thank you to the whole team for their efforts. At least, I have now had some more laps under my belt before going into the race tomorrow, which is a positive considering everything that has happened so far this weekend.

“Q1 felt really good, and I even felt we had the potential to make it into Q3. However, with the track evolving and our balance changing, it became a bit more challenging to adapt, especially given the lack of practice and fine-tuning. It is difficult to predict how tomorrow will pan out for us, but we will try to keep it clean and make the most of our opportunities.”

Allan McNish, Racing Director

“After a very difficult Friday and Saturday morning, the team recovered extremely well, with Nico qualifying P11 and Gabi P14. For Gabi to go straight into qualifying with so little track time and produce that performance was exceptional. Great credit also goes to his mechanics, supported by the crew from Nico’s car, for ensuring his car was ready and giving him the opportunity to deliver. Nico extracted everything we had in the car today, finishing just three hundredths shy and tantalisingly close to a place in Q3. It was a tremendous effort across the team, and those starting positions give us plenty to race for tomorrow.”

Haas

Haas have swapped Esteban Ocon for Ryo Hirakawa for the rest of the race weekend, with the rookie managing plenty of laps in FP3 before embarking on his debut Qualifying session. He gave a good account of himself, winding up around nine tenths behind his team mate after picking up traffic on his final run. Ollie Bearman did make Q2 for the team, but had a messy final lap with one mistake and that cost him a handful of places.

Oliver Bearman, 15th, 1:18.083

“It was a good session, honestly, considering what happened in FP3, which was that we arrived with a car that was just not working at all. Considering that, I think we did a good job, the car felt very good. Especially in Q2, I was on for a really nice lap but made a mistake in Turn 12. It’s a shame, and it’s tough because I’m kind of taking a step into the unknown every time I get into qualifying when we have these FP2 and FP3 sessions when they’re quite disrupted. It’s difficult because the car is quick, we just can’t make it quick in every session, and then it’s challenging to consistently put the car on the edge. I’m excited for tomorrow, let’s see what we can do as the pace looks good and we should be further up the grid than we are.”

Ryo Hirakawa, 19th, 1:18.958

“I’m here to be a reserve driver and am always ready. I’ve dreamt about it, and today, the dream has come true to race tomorrow. Today has flown by, there’s been a lot to prepare, and the team has helped a lot, so thanks to them. For the race, there’s a lot to go through, but today the focus was to try to get through Q1. Unfortunately for me, I had traffic in my last push lap, which is a shame as the car was working well. Tonight, I’ve got a lot of work to do, but I’m excited for the race tomorrow.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“It was a bit of a mixed bag for us today. Ryō was drafted into the car last minute, and I think considering that, he’s done a really good job. In FP3, the progress he was making was very clear, and Q1 is always a very tricky session with the tyre being on the edge, but he stayed calm and managed to extract most of the performance. It’s a shame that he had traffic in the worst possible place, in the high-speed corners. I don’t know if he could’ve made it to Q2, but it would’ve been close. That would’ve been his reward for his great effort today.

“On Ollie’s side, we didn’t maximise everything, which is a shame because his FP1 was very strong, but FP2 and FP3, the car wasn’t where it should be, so he completely lost his reference. We managed however, to get the car back to a good base for qualifying, but that meant he started Q1 run one, like it was FP1 run one. On that note, he had a great Q1, and in Q2, he was making great progress but pushed it too hard into Turn 12. There are a few things we can look at to improve consistency, but I’d like to thank the team for all their hard work and effort, as we’ve had engine changes both days in a short space of time and never missed a session, so that’s a great effort. Starting a bit further back than where we wanted to now, but we will race hard tomorrow to try and get back as many places as possible.”

Williams

Not to be for Alex Albon, who exited in Qualifying at the first time of asking. Carlos Sainz scraped into Q2 but could go no further, the Spaniard left slightly frustrated with the feeling in his Williams. Sainz was also noted for not returning to the track correctly via an escape road at Turn 11, but was let off with a warning. As for Albon, he has qualified very close to Alonso, who he tangled with last time out in Austin. Those two might be worth a watch off the line tomorrow...

Carlos Sainz, 16th, 1:18.885

“We had the chance to get the car into Q2 today. We maximised what we had and took our opportunity, so we can be happy with that. Still, I didn’t feel as comfortable compared to yesterday and I was fighting the car a lot more than usual. We’ve been struggling with balance, and we overcorrected slightly with the setup changes we made. We have faster cars in front and behind us tomorrow, so it will be very tricky to get into the points, but we’ll try our best to put on a good show for these fantastic fans!”

Alex Albon, 17th, 1:18.630

“It was a good lap, maybe my best of the year, so I’m happy with that. Regardless, we'll try to have some fun out there, with the focus being on getting the most out of our car.”

James Vowles, Team Principal

“It was a great lap from Alex. Because of the yellow flag, we had to push right to the limit, and with the traffic he wasn’t able to get his deployment in the right place and lost out on that lap. Aston Martin

The Spaniard could not contain his frustration, as he exited as a result. Lance Stroll also had a tricky day, a PU problem limited his running in practice, before he too dropped out in Q1.

Fernando Alonso, 18th, 1:18.908

“It was a frustrating way to end what had been looking like a promising Qualifying. The car felt good, and we seemed to be in the fight for a place in Q2. Unfortunately, an engine issue meant we had to stop, and there was nothing more we could do at that point. We will look into exactly what happened, but with the cooling challenges we are facing, tomorrow is going to be difficult. We will do what we can and keep pushing as a team.”

Lance Stroll, 20th, 1:19.072

“We have been struggling a bit here all weekend, mainly with the car balance. I also feel something is not quite right at the rear, and we are also struggling with a lot of engine braking issues. Cadillac

Sergio Perez missed almost all of FP3 with Cadillac opting to swap out his power unit as a precautionary measure, but he was able to come out straight away in Q1. He was joined by Valtteri Bottas, who was still playing catch up after missing FP1. “The conditions were changing quite a lot, but I think we managed them reasonably well. Missing FP3 was far from ideal, as we couldn’t test the changes we made to the car before qualifying. Thanks to Valtteri for the tows too, it drew us closer and almost gave us a shot at out qualifying some of the cars ahead.

“Hopefully, we can get a good start tomorrow and fight with the cars ahead. Overtaking is very difficult here, so track position will be key. If we can stay in the mix and keep some faster cars behind us, that would be a positive result.”

“A straightforward qualifying session for us today with everything going to plan. Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal

“More tricks than treats for us today. We got off to a rough start with Checo when we had to change his power unit during FP3 which cost him the whole session. “As Valtteri has a grid penalty tomorrow for running a new PU following his retirement in Austin, he compromised his Qualifying session to help Checo, so thanks to him for being such a great team player. “We approach the Mexico City Grand Prix with a very open strategic picture. The final choice will depend on a range of factors, including each car's characteristics, aerodynamic set-up levels and, above all, the traffic drivers may encounter after a pit stop.

"Many teams may choose to start on the Medium and switch to the Soft between laps 35 and 41, taking it through to the chequered flag. In this scenario, tyre management will remain an important factor despite the relatively low degradation levels. The alternative two-stop strategy would involve starting on the Soft, followed by a stint on the Medium and a final stint once again on the Soft. According to our simulations, there is no significant difference in total race time between these two options. However, teams opting for the two-stop strategy will need to carefully assess the impact of traffic, as the number of cars they may need to overtake after each stop could prove decisive.

"The Hard does not appear to be a particularly competitive choice compared with the main alternatives. title: Lewis Hamilton facing 'guesstimate' for Mexico City GP after practice pain

Lewis Hamilton has suggested he is on the back foot heading into the Mexico City Grand Prix as he targets his second race victory of the season.

The seven-time champion prevailed on Saturday in qualifying, besting former team-mate George Russell to the top of the timesheet.

"In general, I don't think this year I've had a good long run," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

Hamilton under pressure to keep hold of P1

title: FIA issued 'calm down' warning before ill-tempered Verstappen-Lawson clash
excerpt:
Karun Chandhok has revealed that the FIA explicitly told team principals to rein in their drivers during free practice hours before Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson collided in FP2 at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The two collided at Turn 14 when Verstappen, who had gone off the edge of the track, rejoined and made contact with Lawson's front wing, triggering a red flag at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Both drivers were subsequently handed a one-place grid penalty and a penalty point.

Speaking on Sky Sports F1, Chandhok explained the chain of events that led to the clash.

"Now we heard his [Max's] engineer telling him to get ahead of Liam, to get track position ahead of Liam... So that's what Max is trying to do," he said.

"When they get down to this hairpin, Liam has clearly decided he's in no mood to let Max pass. So he comes back down the inside... And I think this has annoyed Max because he thought, 'Well, I'm now in front. You should get out of the way.' Max opts to go beyond the edge of the track... and then sort of just barges into Liam as they come through the right-hander.

"So, the whole thing, in my opinion, just feels a bit unnecessary and a bit clumsy for FP2."

Stewards' warning

Chandhok went on to reveal that stewards had gathered all 11 team bosses that same morning to issue a direct warning over driver conduct in practice sessions.

He also referred to the Esteban Ocon flashpoint that ultimately culminated in the Frenchman being stood down for the weekend at Haas, after a disagreement that stemmed from when the Haas driver vented his frustration over team radio to race engineer Laura Mueller after his run plan was switched from soft to medium tyres.

Haas subsequently withdrew Ocon from the remainder of the weekend, with reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa stepping in, though the team has offered no formal explanation for the decision beyond confirming it was not due to illness.

"I get that in Esteban Ocon's situation, you're trying to get information, you're trying to do the learning, but there's got to be a time and place for this level of aggression," Chandhok added.

"Now, the reason I should point out why they have been penalised. Because in the past we've seen drivers not be penalised for free practice incidents.

"But [on Friday] morning, all of the team managers, 11 team managers, were in a meeting with the stewards, who told them, 'Ask your drivers to behave in free practice.'

"We've seen a few too many incidents in the recent races; we saw Leclerc and George, for example, in Austin, and the stewards have said, 'Look, we're going to start penalising people if they don't behave in free practice.'

"And I think that's why both of these drivers have got that one-place penalty. And really, they both played a part in the way that played out. Although you could say, Max went off the track and barged into him there..."

title: MotoGP manufacturer confirms sensational withdrawal from Qatar round
excerpt:
The conflict in the Middle East has seen one MotoGP manufacturer pull out of the upcoming round from Qatar.

Yamaha has confirmed it will not take part in the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix, citing "company-wide travel restrictions" linked to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The manufacturer issued a statement revealing it has informed MotoGP it does not intend to run its four bikes at the Lusail circuit, with concerns mounting over a potential escalation in the USA-Iran war.

"Following its latest assessment of the situation in the Middle East, Yamaha has not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions," the statement read.

"As a result, Yamaha has informed MotoGP Group about its decision not to participate in the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix.

"This decision reflects Yamaha's assessment of the information currently available and is independent of the measures implemented by MotoGP Group and the event organiser.

"Yamaha remains fully committed to MotoGP and looks forward to returning to competition at the Portuguese Grand Prix."

The statement does not mention specific teams by name, but it is understood to apply to Yamaha's factory outfit as well as partner squad Pramac.

MotoGP warns of 'consequences' after Yamaha withdrawal

MotoGP has issued a response to the news, stating that the non-participation from Yamaha will likely result in 'sporting implications'.

“MotoGP is disappointed by Yamaha's decision not to participate in the Qatar Grand Prix,” it said.

“While we recognise the team is subject to a broader corporate policy restricting travel to the Middle East, we do not believe this decision reflects the extensive assurances provided to all championship stakeholders.

“Following consultation with the State of Qatar, Lusail International Circuit, independent safety advisers and MotoGP's own ongoing risk assessment process, MotoGP has not received any information that would warrant a change to the current plans for the event.

“We communicated that position, together with the latest available information, to all Manufacturers and Teams today and welcome the confirmation from the remainder of the grid that they will compete in Qatar, and we thank them for that commitment.

“In addition to the contractual implications of Yamaha's decision for its agreements with MotoGP and IRTA, Yamaha's non-participation also carries sporting implications, with any sporting consequences to be managed by the FIM in accordance with the Championship regulations.”

title: Fernando Alonso 'frustration beyond imagination' after latest Aston Martin woe
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso described his frustration as "beyond imagination" after another Honda power unit failure wrecked his Mexico City Grand Prix qualifying.

Alonso was forced out of Q1 when his Aston Martin sustained a water pressure issue linked to the energy recovery system.

The two-time F1 champion, who had already shown worrying signs of power loss during final practice, was instructed to stop his car immediately once the problem was detected in Q1 rather than risk terminal damage to the PU.

The team duly pulled him from the session, leaving the 45-year-old 18th on the timesheet. He was also handed a reprimand for failing to re-fit the steering wheel before climbing out of the cockpit.

Alonso explained that stopping on track, rather than attempting to limp back to the garage, was the only sensible option once the fault appeared.

"Yeah, I was 100 metres away from the garage, but probably the problem was bigger than anything possible to do in the garage," said Alonso, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"So the safest thing for everyone else, also on track, was to stop, and I followed this direction."

[Article continues below]

Alonso - 'The story of the year'

Asked whether a place in Q3 had been realistic before the car failed, Alonso suggested the pace was there, if not the result.

"Probably difficult, but yeah, we were P12, P13, P11, so we were in the window," he said. "If we had put in a good one, maybe it was possible. But I think that was probably too optimistic. Maybe P13, P12 was our position."

The Aston Martin driver has dismissed any suggestion he could now fight forward from the back of the grid at a circuit where cooling and altitude have already punished the team's package throughout the weekend.

"No, no, no," he insisted. "Here, there are huge problems with temperatures for everybody, so when you start at the back, there is no way you can follow cars closely. There is not much we can do.

"I think we lost a big opportunity, so frustration is beyond imagination, but this is the story of the year."

Alonso also pointed to the layout of the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez as a reason the AMR26 had looked more competitive than usual over the weekend.

"Fewer straights," he said. "There are only two straights, into Turn 1, into Turn 4. The rest, with the level of grip being so low, you hardly go full throttle, so it is less power sensitive here. So maybe because of that."

Asked whether he would now need a fresh power unit for the race, a disconsolate Alonso gave a blunt reply: "I don't know. I guess so."

Honda has confirmed it will be changing components on Alonso's PU, so it is certain he will be handed a penalty.

title: Lewis Hamilton recalls Michael Schumacher memories after first Ferrari pole
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has drawn a direct line between his first Ferrari pole position and memories of watching Michael Schumacher dominate qualifying for the Scuderia, after ending a three-year wait for the top spot on the grid in Mexico City.

The seven-time world champion topped qualifying at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez with a lap of one minute 16.514s, edging out Mercedes' George Russell by just 0.009 seconds. Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc will start third.

It is Hamilton's first pole since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, a gap stretching to 78 race weekends. At 41, he also becomes the oldest polesitter since Mario Andretti in the 1982 Italian GP.

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Hamilton confirmed the achievement carried extra emotional weight given his history with the sport's most successful Ferrari driver.

"It definitely does [matter a lot]," Hamilton said. "It's been a long time since I think I've sat in this spot. I don't really remember the last time I had a pole.

"Embarking on this journey with Ferrari and all the challenges and ups and downs we've had, and even yesterday was challenging, obviously, when the car stopped on track, and we lost the long run that everyone got to do.

"But just continuing to hold on to that hope that one day we'll get back on the front row and to P1 once we dialled the car in.

Extolling his "belief in this team, the opportunity that they've given me and the belief and faith they've put in me", he proclaimed it "great to be able to reward them with a pole".

He then pertinently added: "And to have your first Ferrari pole, it just takes me back to watching Michael get all those pole positions when he was at Ferrari and all those wins. So, it's very, very special."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton had to be "millimetre perfect"

Hamilton also detailed the margins involved in beating Leclerc to the top spot, with the Monégasque setting the pace on the first runs in Q3 before the Briton found more on his final attempt.

"It was such a close qualifying and so difficult, I think, for everyone, working the tyres," he said. "So little downforce and grip that you have on here, so you just have to be as millimetre perfect as you can be.

"It was a really, really clean lap. I needed it because Charles was three or four tenths up the road from the first run, and that's quite a big deficit to close on your last lap.

"But I knew areas that I could improve on. I just got the tyres in the perfect window on that out-lap. Once I was through Turns 1, 2 and 3, it was kind of smooth from there, and I just don't think I lost any time anywhere, to be honest.

"So, it was just an overall good lap, but I know these guys are super close."

title: Liam Lawson issues apology as Jenson Button makes case for extended F1 stay

Liam Lawson has revealed to apologising to Max Verstappen after the pair collided during second practice for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The two drivers made contact at Turn 14, with Verstappen's Red Bull and Lawson's Racing Bulls machinery both suffering damage. The incident triggered a red flag and left both drivers with one-place grid penalties for Sunday's race at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

The clash came as a surprise given the relationship between the two, with Verstappen having previously backed Lawson internally during his time in the Red Bull setup.

Lawson made clear he had gone to clear the air with the four-time F1 champion before Saturday's running.

"It's not ideal," said Lawson. "I went to see Max to apologise because what happened doesn't need to happen.

"I don't want to have that happen in the future. Obviously, right now, it's not the best time, so yeah, it's been a tricky day, honestly.

"But I'm happy to drive the car. At the moment, I just like driving the car."

Despite qualifying eighth fastest, and dropping a place to ninth because of the penalty, the day ended even more sourly for Lawson, however, after being disqualified from qualifying for a technical breach.

Button weighs in on Lawson future

The clash has come at a sensitive moment for Lawson, with his Racing Bulls future still unresolved.

Junior driver Nikola Tsolov, who sits second in the F2 standings, took over Lawson's car in first practice in Mexico as part of the team's evaluation process.

Jenson Button, the 2009 F1 champion, has made it clear where his sympathies lie, pointing to Lawson's season-long consistency over the promise Tsolov has shown.

"It's such a difficult one for the team to call," said Button. "They obviously have the junior Tsolov coming through in F2, second in the championship, doing an amazing job.

"But he's also had inconsistencies through his years. He's had moments of brilliance, but then he's had other races where it's not quite been there for him.

"Maybe the team are excited about getting young new talent in the team, but I think Liam's job this year has been really good. He's been very consistent.

"They know what they're getting with Liam, whereas with Tsolov, they don't. So maybe they're excited about that. I don't know.

"But if they're there to score points at the moment, I would say Liam's your guy."

title: Liam Lawson disqualified after Mexico City qualifying for F1 technical breach
excerpt:
Liam Lawson is going to need a major Mexico City comeback to score points.

Liam Lawson has been disqualified from qualifying for the Mexico City Grand Prix after stewards ruled his Racing Bulls car breached technical regulations, scrubbing his eighth-place in qualifying.

Lawson entered qualifying already with a one-place grid penalty following his incident with Max Verstappen in second practice on Friday, but now moves all the way to the very back of the grid.

The New Zealander's car was referred to the stewards by the FIA's technical delegate almost immediately after qualifying, who found that Lawson's car was "in breach of the minimum MGU-K power requirement just after crossing the line on his fastest lap in Q2 at 15:47:36.

"This is a breach of Articles C5.12.6 and C5.12.7. The driver maximum power demand and the electrical DC power of the ERS-K were reduced at greater rates than what is permitted by the regulations."

Shortly after the referral, Lawson was summoned to the stewards, with the announcement of his disqualification from qualifying coming shortly after.

Lawson's elimination from the results means he will need the stewards' permission to take part in the race on Sunday. That approval is routinely granted on the basis of times set in free practice, meaning the his participation is not in serious doubt.

Where he lines up is a separate matter. A driver excluded from qualifying normally starts from the back of the grid, unless his Racing Bulls squad breaches parc fermé rules by altering the car's setup or swapping components, in which case he would instead have to start from the pit lane.

Either scenario would hand Racing Bulls the option to fit any tyre compound for the opening stint and introduce power unit parts without the usual grid penalty consequences, an approach teams have used before at the high-altitude Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez to run an extended first stint on the hard tyre.

The full stewards' reasoning for Liam Lawson disqualification

The stewards' report read: "The stewards heard from the team representatives of Car 30 (Liam Lawson), the driver, the single seater sporting director and members of the FIA technical team including the FIA technical delegate.

"Evidence submitted, which was accepted by all parties present, showed that after the control line at the end of his fastest lap in Q2, the driver did not lift off the power immediately. This resulted in the rate of reduction of MGUK deployment required to achieve the regulated “step down”, not being achieved.

"The team argued that this did not provide any performance advantage however it is clear that non-compliance with the technical regulations is not excused if no performance advantage is gained. Further, these regulations require that a car must comply with them at all times during an event.

"The stewards note in particular that the team self-disclosed the breach however there are a multitude of precedents that require us, despite all mitigating circumstances, to impose a penalty of disqualification where a car does not comply with the technical regulations."
